#### Frame timer sample code

To count frames a simple timer can be created as follows:


In both of these examples, the timer will be automatically discarded once it is finished. Set discardOnCompletion to false to keep the timer around for later reuse.

An example of setting up a bouncing ball animation (assuming the ball would be drawn elsewhere based on the rectangle r):

### 7.32. UI components

playdate.ui provides common UI elements for playdate games.

#### Crank indicator

`playdate.ui.crankIndicator` is used to draw a standard indicator at the lower right corner of the screen that directs the player to use the crank.

As your game calls`playdate.ui.crankIndicator:draw()` on successive frames, the Playdate screen will display a "Use the Crank" message for ~0.7 seconds, then an animation of a rotating crank for ~1.4 seconds. (The direction of animation is specified by`.clockwise`.)

In some situations you may only want to alert the player to "use the crank" if`playdate.isCrankDocked()` returns`true`, indicating that the crank is not extended.

Important

| You must import CoreLibs/ui to use crankIndicator. There is no need to instantiate a crankIndicator object;`playdate.ui.crankIndicator` automatically returns the shared crankIndicator instance. |
| --- |

playdate.ui.crankIndicator:draw([xOffset, yOffset])

Draws the next frame of the crank indicator animation, and is typically invoked in the`playdate.update()` callback. xOffset and yOffset can be used to alter the position of the indicator by a specified number of pixels if desired. To stop drawing the crank indicator, simply stop calling`:draw()` in`playdate.update()`.

Note that if sprites are being used, this call should usually happen after playdate.graphics.sprite.update().

playdate.ui.crankIndicator.clockwise

Boolean property specifying which direction to animate the crank. Defaults to true.

playdate.ui.crankIndicator:resetAnimation()

Resets the crank animation to the beginning of its sequence.

playdate.ui.crankIndicator:getBounds()

Returns x, y, width, height representing the bounds that the crank indicator draws within. If necessary, this rect could be passed into playdate.graphics.sprite.addDirtyRect(), or used to manually draw over the indicator image drawn by playdate.ui.crankIndicator:draw() when you want to stop showing the crank indicator.

#### Grid view

playdate.ui.gridview provides a means for drawing a grid view composed of cells, and optionally sections with section headers.

Important

| You must import CoreLibs/ui to use gridview. |
| --- |

Some notes:

playdate.ui.gridview uses playdate.timer internally, so playdate.timer.updateTimers() must be called in the main playdate.update() function.

If the gridview’s cell width is set to 0, cells will be drawn the same width as the table (minus any padding).

Section headers always draw the full width of the grid (minus padding), and do not scroll horizontally along with the rest of the content.

playdate.ui.gridview.new(cellWidth, cellHeight)

Returns a new playdate.ui.gridview with cells sized cellWidth, cellHeight. (Sizes are in pixels.) If cells should span the entire width of the grid (as in a list view), pass zero (0) for cellWidth.

##### Drawing

playdate.ui.gridview:drawCell(section, row, column, selected, x, y, width, height)

Override this method to draw the cells in the gridview. selected is a boolean, true if the cell being drawn is the currently-selected cell.

playdate.ui.gridview:drawSectionHeader(section, x, y, width, height)

Override this method to draw section headers. This function will only be called if the header height has been set to a value greater than zero (0).

playdate.ui.gridview:drawHorizontalDivider(x, y, width, height)

Override this method to customize the drawing of horizontal dividers. This function will only be called if the horizontal divider height is greater than zero (0) and at least one divider has been added.

playdate.ui.gridview:drawInRect(x, y, width, height)

Draws the gridview in the specified rect. Ideally this should be called on every playdate.update() to accommodate scrolling.

playdate.ui.gridview.needsDisplay

This read-only variable returns true if the gridview needs to be redrawn. This can be used to help optimize drawing in your app. Keep in mind that a gridview cannot know all reasons it may need to be redrawn, such as changes in your drawing callback functions, coordinate or size changes, or overlapping drawing, so you may need to additionally redraw at other times.

Conditionally draw a grid view

```
if myGridView.needsDisplay == true then
    myGridView:drawInRect(x, y, w, h)
end
```

##### Configuration

playdate.ui.gridview:setNumberOfSections(num)

Sets the number of sections in the grid view. Each section contains at least one row, and row numbering starts at 1 in each section.

playdate.ui.gridview:getNumberOfSections()

Returns the number of sections in the grid view.

playdate.ui.gridview:setNumberOfRowsInSection(section, num)

Sets the number of rows in section.

playdate.ui.gridview:getNumberOfRowsInSection(section)

Returns the number of rows in section.

playdate.ui.gridview:setNumberOfColumns(num)

Sets the number of columns in the gridview. 1 by default.

playdate.ui.gridview:getNumberOfColumns()

Returns the number of columns in the gridview. 1 by default.

playdate.ui.gridview:setNumberOfRows(…​)

Convenience method for list-style gridviews, or for setting the number of rows for multiple sections at a time. Pass in a list of numbers of rows for sections starting from section 1.

playdate.ui.gridview:setCellSize(cellWidth, cellHeight)

Sets the size of the cells in the gridview. If cells should span the entire width of the grid (as in a list view), pass zero (0) for cellWidth.

playdate.ui.gridview:setCellPadding(left, right, top, bottom)

Sets the amount of padding around cells.

playdate.ui.gridview:setContentInset(left, right, top, bottom)

Sets the amount of space the content is inset from the edges of the gridview. Useful if a background image is being used as a border.

playdate.ui.gridview:getCellBounds(section, row, column, [gridWidth])

Returns multiple values (x, y, width, height) representing the bounds of the cell, not including padding, relative to the top-right corner of the grid view.

If the grid view is configured with zero width cells (see playdate.ui.gridview:new), gridWidth is required, and should be the same value you would pass to playdate.ui.gridview:drawInRect.

playdate.ui.gridview:setSectionHeaderHeight(height)

Sets the height of the section headers. 0 by default, which causes section headers not to be drawn.

playdate.ui.gridview.getSectionHeaderHeight()

Returns the current height of the section headers.

playdate.ui.gridview:setSectionHeaderPadding(left, right, top, bottom)

Sets the amount of padding around section headers.

playdate.ui.gridview:setHorizontalDividerHeight(height)

Sets the height of the horizontal dividers. The default height is half the cell height specified when creating the grid view.

playdate.ui.gridview:getHorizontalDividerHeight()

Returns the height of the horizontal dividers.

playdate.ui.gridview:addHorizontalDividerAbove(section, row)

Causes a horizontal divider to be drawn above the specified row. Drawing can be customized by overriding playdate.ui.gridview:drawHorizontalDivider.

playdate.ui.gridview:removeHorizontalDividers()

Removes all horizontal dividers from the grid view.

playdate.ui.gridview:setScrollDuration(ms)

Controls the duration of scroll animations. 250ms by default.

playdate.ui.gridview:setScrollPosition(x, y, [animated])

'set' scrolls to the coordinate x, y.

If animated is true (or not provided) the new scroll position is animated to using playdate.ui.gridview.scrollEasingFunction and the value set in playdate.ui.gridview:setScrollDuration().

playdate.ui.gridview:getScrollPosition()

Returns the current scroll location as a pair x, y.

playdate.ui.gridview:scrollToCell(section, row, column, [animated])

Scrolls to the specified cell, just enough so the cell is visible.

Scrolls to the specified cell, so the cell is centered in the gridview, if possible.

Convenience function for list-style gridviews. Scrolls to the specified row in the list.

playdate.ui.gridview:scrollToTop([animated])

Scrolls to the top of the gridview.

##### Selection

Changing the selection can also change the scroll position. By default cells are scrolled so that they are centered in the gridview, if possible. To change that behavior so the grid is just scrolled enough to make the cell visible, set scrollCellsToCenter to false.

playdate.ui.gridview:setSelection(section, row, column)

Selects the cell at the given position.

playdate.ui.gridview:getSelection()

Returns the currently-selected cell as section, row, column

playdate.ui.gridview:setSelectedRow(row)

Convenience method for list-style gridviews. Selects the cell at row in section 1.

playdate.ui.gridview:getSelectedRow()

Convenience method for list-style gridviews. Returns the selected cell at row in section 1.

playdate.ui.gridview:selectNextRow(wrapSelection, [scrollToSelection, animate])

Selects the cell directly below the currently-selected cell.

If wrapSelection is true, the selection will wrap around to the opposite end of the grid. If scrollToSelection is true (or not provided), the newly-selected cell will be scrolled to. If animate is true (or not provided), the scroll will be animated.

playdate.ui.gridview:selectPreviousRow(wrapSelection, [scrollToSelection, animate])

Identical to`selectNextRow()` but goes the other direction.

Selects the cell directly to the right of the currently-selected cell.

If the last column is currently selected and wrapSelection is true, the selection will wrap around to the opposite side of the grid. If a wrap occurs and the gridview’s`changeRowOnColumnWrap` is`true` the row will also be advanced or moved back.

Identical to`selectNextColumn()` but goes the other direction.

playdate.ui.gridview.backgroundImage

A background image that draws behind the gridview’s cells. This image can be either a`playdate.graphics.image` which will be tiled or a`playdate.nineSlice`.

Read-only. True if the gridview is currently performing a scroll animation.

The easing function used when performing scroll animations. The function should be of the form function(t, b, c, d), where t is elapsed time, b is the beginning value, c is the change, or end value - start value, and d is the duration. ##### Grid view sample code

To set up a grid view, specify the dimensions and override the necessary drawing methods:

Grid view example

```
local gfx = playdate.graphics
local gridview = playdate.ui.gridview.new(44, 44)
gridview.backgroundImage = playdate.graphics.nineSlice.new('shadowbox', 4, 4, 45, 45)
gridview:setNumberOfColumns(8)
gridview:setNumberOfRows(2, 4, 3, 5) -- number of sections is set automatically
gridview:setSectionHeaderHeight(24)
gridview:setContentInset(1, 4, 1, 4)
gridview:setCellPadding(4, 4, 4, 4)
gridview.changeRowOnColumnWrap = false

function gridview:drawCell(section, row, column, selected, x, y, width, height)
    if selected then
        gfx.drawCircleInRect(x-2, y-2, width+4, height+4, 3)
    else
        gfx.drawCircleInRect(x+4, y+4, width-8, height-8, 0)
    end
    local cellText = ""..row.."-"..column
    gfx.drawTextInRect(cellText, x, y+14, width, 20, nil, nil, kTextAlignment.center)
end

function gridview:drawSectionHeader(section, x, y, width, height)
    gfx.drawText("*SECTION ".. section .. "*", x + 10, y + 8)
end
```

For the simple case of a simple list-style grid:

List-style grid view example

```
local menuOptions = {"Sword", "Shield", "Arrow", "Sling", "Stone", "Longbow", "MorningStar", "Armour", "Dagger", "Rapier", "Skeggox", "War Hammer", "Battering Ram", "Catapult"}
local listview = playdate.ui.gridview.new(0, 10)
listview.backgroundImage = playdate.graphics.nineSlice.new('scrollbg', 20, 23, 92, 28)
listview:setNumberOfRows(#menuOptions)
listview:setCellPadding(0, 0, 13, 10)
listview:setContentInset(24, 24, 13, 11)

function listview:drawCell(section, row, column, selected, x, y, width, height)
        if selected then
                gfx.fillRoundRect(x, y, width, 20, 4)
                gfx.setImageDrawMode(gfx.kDrawModeFillWhite)
        else
                gfx.setImageDrawMode(gfx.kDrawModeCopy)
        end
        gfx.drawTextInRect(menuOptions[row], x, y+2, width, height, nil, "...", kTextAlignment.center)
end
```

Then, to draw the grid view:

Drawing a grid view

```
function playdate.update()
    gridview:drawInRect(20, 20, 180, 200)
    listview:drawInRect(220, 20, 160, 210)
    playdate.timer:updateTimers()
end
```

### 7.35. Garbage collection

playdate.setCollectsGarbage(flag)

If flag is false, automatic garbage collection is disabled and the game should manually collect garbage with Lua’s`collectgarbage()` function.

playdate.setMinimumGCTime(ms)

Force the Lua garbage collector to run for at least ms milliseconds every frame, so that garbage doesn’t pile up and cause the game to run out of memory and stall in emergency garbage collection. The default value is 1 millisecond.

Tip

| If your game isn’t generating a lot of garbage, it might be advantageous to set a smaller minimum GC time, granting more CPU bandwidth to your game. |
| --- |

playdate.setGCScaling(min, max)

When the amount of used memory is less than`min`(scaled from 0-1, as a percentage of total system memory), the system will only run the collector for the minimum GC time, as set by playdate.setGCScaling(), every frame. If the used memory is more than`max`, the system will spend all free time running the collector. Between the two, the time used by the garbage collector is scaled proportionally.

For example, if the scaling is set to a min of 0.4 and max of 0.7, and memory is half full, the collector will run for the minimum GC time plus 1/3 of whatever time is left before the next frame (because (0.5 - 0.4) / (0.7 - 0.4) = 1/3).

The default behavior is a scaling of`(0.0, 1.0)`. If set to`(0.0, 0.0)`, the system will use all available extra time each frame running GC.

## 8. Hidden Gems

The Playdate APIs include a lot of functionality you might expect:

graphics

sprites

collisions

animation

sound

file I/O

localization

There are also some unexpected APIs, some unique to the Playdate platform, that you may not be aware of. Be sure to take a look at these:

### 8.1. Lua enhancements

The Playdate SDK offers some enhancements to standard Lua, including additional assignment operators (`+=`,`-=`) and convenience functions for handling Lua tables.

### 8.2. Debugging

playdate.drawFPS(): Displays the current framerate onscreen.

playdate.debugDraw(): Highlight regions on the Simulator screen in a different color, to aid in debugging.

printTable(): Outputs the contents of a table to the console.

playdate.keyPressed(): Captures computer keyboard keypresses as an aid in debugging. For example, typing a number might advance the game to a higher level.

### 8.3. Enhancing your game’s user experience

playdate.ui.crankIndicator(): Inform the player that your game uses the crank.

playdate.menu:addOptionsMenuItem(): Add a special menu item for your game into the System Menu.

playdate.wait(): Pause your game’s execution for a specified period of time. Useful for, say, suspending gameplay while displaying a message to the player.

playdate.setMenuImage(): Set a custom image that displays on the left-side of the screen while your game is paused.

playdate.keyboard: Display a special Playdate keyboard onscreen and collect text input from the player.

playdate.timer.keyRepeatTimer(): Useful, keyboard-style repeating.

### 8.4. Buttons

playdate.AButtonHeld(), playdate.BButtonHeld(): Called after the A or B buttons are held for one second. Useful for adding a "second function" to a button (display a map, for instance).

### 8.5. Responding to device events

content.text:
Good questions. Let me answer them and probe the game state capability:

## DAP Protocol Basics

DAP is simple: TCP socket, newline-delimited JSON messages with `Content-Length` framing (same as LSP).

**Message format:**
```
Content-Length: 42\r\n
\r\n
{"seq":1,"type":"request","command":"initialize","arguments":{}}
```

Three message types: `request` (client→server), `response` (server→client), `event` (server→client, async).

**Session lifecycle:**
1. Connect TCP to `localhost:55934`
2. Send `initialize` request → get capabilities response
3. Send `configurationDone` → server confirms, sends `process` event
4. Now you can send `evaluate` requests freely
5. Connection persists until you close the socket or the simulator exits

**Connection model:** It's a persistent TCP connection. You connect once, send as many commands as you want. No auth, no session tokens. The simulator only accepts one client at a time (second connection likely gets ignored or queued).

**Library needed?** No. The protocol is trivial -- just `net.Socket` from Node.js with a small framer. The framing is identical to LSP: read `Content-Length` header, read that many bytes, JSON.parse. We don't need `vscode-debugadapter` or any DAP library.

For our extension, I'd build a small `DapClient` class in `src/lib/dap.ts` (~100 lines) that:
- Manages the TCP connection lifecycle
- Handles send/receive with sequence numbering
- Exposes `evaluate(expr): Promise<string>` as the main method
- Auto-reconnects if the simulator restarts

Now let me probe what game state we can read:

    { { 2, 1 }, { 2, 2 }, { 2, 3 } },
    { { 3, 1 }, { 3, 2 }, { 3, 3 } },
    { { 1, 1 }, { 2, 1 }, { 3, 1 } },
    { { 1, 2 }, { 2, 2 }, { 3, 2 } },
    { { 1, 3 }, { 2, 3 }, { 3, 3 } },
    { { 1, 1 }, { 2, 2 }, { 3, 3 } },
    { { 1, 3 }, { 2, 2 }, { 3, 1 } },
}

local board = {}
local cursorX = 2
local cursorY = 2
local currentPlayer = humanPlayer
local gameOver = false
local winner = nil

local function resetGame()
    board = {
        { nil, nil, nil },
        { nil, nil, nil },
        { nil, nil, nil },
    }

    cursorY = 2
    currentPlayer = humanPlayer
    gameOver = false
    winner = nil
    print("reset game")

        for col = 1, 3 do
            if state[row][col] == nil then
                return false
            end
        end
    end
    return true
end

local function detectWinner(state)
    for _, line in ipairs(lines) do
        local a = line[1]
        local b = line[2]
        local c = line[3]
        local first = state[a[1]][a[2]]

        if first ~= nil
            and first == state[b[1]][b[2]]
            and first == state[c[1]][c[2]] then
            return first
        end
    end

    return nil
end

local function updateGameState()

    cursorY = math.max(1, math.min(3, cursorY + dy))
end

end

local function minimax(state, player, depth)

                    nextState[row][col] = computerPlayer
                    local score = minimax(nextState, humanPlayer, depth + 1)

                    end
                end
            end
        end

    end

    local bestScore = math.huge

    for row = 1, 3 do

                end
            end
        end
    end

end

local function findBestMove()

end

end

local function placeMark()

end

    elseif winner == computerPlayer then

    elseif gameOver then
        status = "Draw"
    elseif currentPlayer == humanPlayer then
        status = "Your turn"
    else

    end

    gfx.drawText("B: reset", 24, 218)

function playdate.downButtonDown()
    moveCursor(0, 1)

    placeMark()

function playdate.BButtonDown()

arguments.instructions:
Create `src/lib/dap.ts` -- a lightweight DAP client for communicating with the Playdate Simulator's debug server on TCP port 55934.

The DAP protocol uses `Content-Length: N\r\n\r\nJSON` framing over TCP (same as LSP).

The client should:

1. **Class `DapClient`** with these properties:
   - `private socket: net.Socket | null`
   - `private seq: number` (auto-incrementing sequence counter)
   - `private pending: Map<number, { resolve, reject, timer }>` (pending request callbacks)
   - `private buffer: Buffer` (incoming data buffer for framing)
   - `private connected: boolean`
   - `private injected: boolean` (whether helpers have been injected)

2. **`connect(port?: number): Promise<void>`** 
   - Default port 55934
   - Creates `net.Socket`, connects
   - Sets up `data` handler that calls `onData` for framing
   - Sets up `close`/`error` handlers that clear state
   - After connect, sends `initialize` request, waits for response
   - Sends `configurationDone`, waits for response
   - Calls `injectHelpers()`

3. **`disconnect(): void`**
   - Destroys socket, clears pending, resets state

4. **`isConnected(): boolean`**

5. **Private `send(command: string, args?: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<DapResponse>`**
   - Increments seq, builds request message `{ seq, type: "request", command, arguments }`
   - JSON encodes, wraps with `Content-Length: N\r\n\r\n`
   - Writes to socket
   - Returns a promise that resolves when a response with matching `request_seq` arrives
   - 10 second timeout, rejects on timeout

6. **Private `onData(chunk: Buffer)`**
   - Appends to buffer
   - Parse loop: find `\r\n\r\n`, extract Content-Length, read body bytes, JSON.parse
   - For each parsed message:
     - If type "response" and has matching request_seq in pending: resolve the pending promise
     - If type "event": ignore (we don't need events for now)

7. **`evaluate(expression: string): Promise<DapEvalResult>`**
   - Calls `send("evaluate", { expression, context: "repl" })`
   - Returns `{ success: boolean, result?: string, output?: string }` 
   - `result` comes from `body.result`, `output` comes from stdout event (if any)
   - Note: the simulator sends `output` events for print() calls BEFORE the evaluate response. To capture these, collect any `output` events that arrive between the request and response. Simplest approach: just use the response body. The response has `body.result` for `p` commands and `body: null` + `message` for errors.

8. **`evalLua(code: string): Promise<string>`**
   - Shorthand: calls `evaluate("eval " + code)`
   - Returns the result string or throws on error

9. **`printExpr(expression: string): Promise<string>`**
   - Shorthand: calls `evaluate("p " + expression)`
   - Returns the result string

10. **`screenshot(outputPath: string): Promise<void>`**
    - Calls `evalLua('playdate.simulator.writeToFile(playdate.graphics.getDisplayImage(), "' + outputPath + '")')`

11. **Private `injectHelpers(): Promise<void>`**
    - If already injected, return
    - Injects a small Lua table serializer as a global `__pd_inspect`:
    ```lua
    function __pd_inspect(v, depth)
      depth = depth or 3
    ```

details.instructions:
Create `src/lib/dap.ts` -- a lightweight DAP client for communicating with the Playdate Simulator's debug server on TCP port 55934.

The DAP protocol uses `Content-Length: N\r\n\r\nJSON` framing over TCP (same as LSP).

The client should:

1. **Class `DapClient`** with these properties:
   - `private socket: net.Socket | null`
   - `private seq: number` (auto-incrementing sequence counter)
   - `private pending: Map<number, { resolve, reject, timer }>` (pending request callbacks)
   - `private buffer: Buffer` (incoming data buffer for framing)
   - `private connected: boolean`
   - `private injected: boolean` (whether helpers have been injected)

2. **`connect(port?: number): Promise<void>`** 
   - Default port 55934
   - Creates `net.Socket`, connects
   - Sets up `data` handler that calls `onData` for framing
   - Sets up `close`/`error` handlers that clear state
   - After connect, sends `initialize` request, waits for response
   - Sends `configurationDone`, waits for response
   - Calls `injectHelpers()`

3. **`disconnect(): void`**
   - Destroys socket, clears pending, resets state

4. **`isConnected(): boolean`**

5. **Private `send(command: string, args?: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<DapResponse>`**
   - Increments seq, builds request message `{ seq, type: "request", command, arguments }`
   - JSON encodes, wraps with `Content-Length: N\r\n\r\n`
   - Writes to socket
   - Returns a promise that resolves when a response with matching `request_seq` arrives
   - 10 second timeout, rejects on timeout

6. **Private `onData(chunk: Buffer)`**
   - Appends to buffer
   - Parse loop: find `\r\n\r\n`, extract Content-Length, read body bytes, JSON.parse
   - For each parsed message:
     - If type "response" and has matching request_seq in pending: resolve the pending promise
     - If type "event": ignore (we don't need events for now)

7. **`evaluate(expression: string): Promise<DapEvalResult>`**
   - Calls `send("evaluate", { expression, context: "repl" })`
   - Returns `{ success: boolean, result?: string, output?: string }` 
   - `result` comes from `body.result`, `output` comes from stdout event (if any)
   - Note: the simulator sends `output` events for print() calls BEFORE the evaluate response. To capture these, collect any `output` events that arrive between the request and response. Simplest approach: just use the response body. The response has `body.result` for `p` commands and `body: null` + `message` for errors.

8. **`evalLua(code: string): Promise<string>`**
   - Shorthand: calls `evaluate("eval " + code)`
   - Returns the result string or throws on error

9. **`printExpr(expression: string): Promise<string>`**
   - Shorthand: calls `evaluate("p " + expression)`
   - Returns the result string

10. **`screenshot(outputPath: string): Promise<void>`**
    - Calls `evalLua('playdate.simulator.writeToFile(playdate.graphics.getDisplayImage(), "' + outputPath + '")')`

11. **Private `injectHelpers(): Promise<void>`**
    - If already injected, return
    - Injects a small Lua table serializer as a global `__pd_inspect`:
    ```lua
    function __pd_inspect(v, depth)
      depth = depth or 3
      if depth <= 0 then return tostring(v) end
      local t = type(v)
      if t ~= "table" then return tostring(v) end
      local parts = {}
      local arr = #v > 0
      if arr then
        for i = 1, math.min(#v, 50) do
          parts[#parts+1] = __pd_inspect(v[i], depth - 1)
        end
        if #v > 50 then parts[#parts+1] = "..." end
      else
        local count = 0
        for k, val in pairs(v) do
          if count >= 50 then parts[#parts+1] = "..."; break end
          parts[#parts+1] = tostring(k) .. "=" .. __pd_inspect(val, depth - 1)
          count = count + 1
        end
      end
      return "{" .. table.concat(parts, ", ") .. "}"
    end
    ```
    - Sets `injected = true`

12. **Interface `DapResponse`**: `{ seq: number, type: string, command: string, success: boolean, message?: string, body?: Record<string, unknown> }`

13. **Interface `DapEvalResult`**: `{ success: boolean, result?: string, output?: string }`

14. **Export `const DAP_PORT = 55934`**

Important implementation notes:
- Use `import { Socket, createConnection } from "node:net"` (NOT child_process, NOT pi.exec)
- The `onData` framing needs to handle partial messages (buffer until complete)
- The `onData` also needs to handle multiple messages in one chunk
- The evaluate response for `eval` commands has `body.result = "Eval complete."` on success
- The evaluate response for `p` commands has `body.result = "<value>"` 
- On error, `success: false` and `message` contains the error string
- Output events (from print()) arrive as separate messages with `type: "event"`, `event: "output"`, `body.output: "text\n"`. For now, we don't need to capture these separately -- the sim_log tool handles stdout. Just ignore events in the pending resolution.

Do NOT use child_process or pi.exec. This is pure TCP via `node:net`.

---
name: playdate
description: Develop games for the Panic Playdate handheld using the pi-playdate extension. Use when the user wants to create, build, run, or debug a Playdate game in Lua or C, work with .pdx bundles, run the Simulator, take screenshots of a running game, or deploy to a connected Playdate device over USB.
---

# Playdate Development

This skill teaches you how to develop games for the Panic Playdate using the `pi-playdate` extension. All Playdate operations go through the `playdate_*` tools -- never shell out to `pdc`, `pdutil`, `cmake`, or any SDK binary directly.

## Available Tools

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `playdate_doctor` | Check SDK installation and environment health |
| `playdate_build` | Compile project to .pdx bundle |
| `playdate_run_sim` | Launch the Playdate Simulator |
| `playdate_stop_sim` | Stop the running simulator |
| `playdate_sim_log` | Read simulator log output |
| `playdate_screenshot` | Capture simulator screenshot |
| `playdate_sim_input` | Send D-pad/A/B/menu input to the simulator |
| `playdate_sim_eval` | Evaluate Lua in the running simulator (read state, run code) |
| `playdate_run_device` | Deploy to a connected Playdate device |

## Creating a New Project

There is no scaffolding tool. Create project files directly using `write`.

Read the appropriate template reference before creating:

- **Lua project**: Read [references/templates-lua.md](references/templates-lua.md) for the required files and their contents.
- **C project**: Read [references/templates-c.md](references/templates-c.md) for the required files, CMakeLists.txt setup, and C API boilerplate.

Every project needs a `Source/pdxinfo` file. See [references/project-layout.md](references/project-layout.md) for the format.

## Typical Workflows

### New game (Lua)

1. Read `references/templates-lua.md`
2. Create `Source/main.lua` and `Source/pdxinfo` using `write`
3. `playdate_build`
4. `playdate_run_sim`
5. `playdate_screenshot` to check visuals
6. `playdate_sim_input` to interact with the game (D-pad, A, B buttons)
7. Edit code, rebuild, repeat

### New game (C)

1. Read `references/templates-c.md`
2. Create `src/main.c`, `Source/pdxinfo`, and `CMakeLists.txt` using `write`
3. `playdate_build` (auto-detects C project and uses CMake)
4. `playdate_run_sim`

### Debug loop

1. `playdate_build` -- check `details.errors` for issues
2. If errors, fix the source files and rebuild
3. `playdate_run_sim` to test
4. `playdate_sim_log` to check runtime output
5. `playdate_screenshot` to verify visuals
6. Iterate

### Deploy to device

1. `playdate_build` with target "device"
2. `playdate_run_device` (always prompts user for confirmation)

## Environment Setup

Run `playdate_doctor` first to verify the SDK is installed and configured. If the SDK path is not auto-detected, the user can set it via `/playdate:settings`.

## Reference Files

For API details, read the reference files in this skill's `references/` directory:

- `project-layout.md` -- Playdate project structure and pdxinfo format
- `templates-lua.md` -- Lua project template with minimal playdate.update()
- `templates-c.md` -- C project template with CMakeLists.txt and event handler
- `lua-api.md` -- Lua API quick reference
- `c-api.md` -- C API quick reference
- `corelibs.md` -- Standard Lua libraries (sprites, graphics, timers, etc.)
- `performance.md` -- Performance tips for the Playdate hardware
- `patterns.md` -- Common game patterns and idioms

edits.newText:
### Interacting with a running game

1. `playdate_sim_input` to send D-pad, A, B, or menu button presses
2. `playdate_screenshot` to see the current display (clean 400x240, no chrome)
3. `playdate_sim_eval` to read or modify game state at runtime

`playdate_sim_input` and `playdate_screenshot` use DAP (Debug Adapter Protocol) when connected, which is more reliable than OS-level automation. DAP connects automatically when the simulator starts a Lua game.

### Reading game state without vision

For models without vision or when you need structured data:

- Use `playdate_sim_eval` with `p <expression>` to read values: `p score`, `p playerX`
- Use `__pd_inspect(table)` to pretty-print tables: `p __pd_inspect(board)`
- `__pd_inspect` is injected automatically by the extension -- no game code changes needed

For richer state access, add a `getState()` global to the game during scaffolding:

```lua
-- Expose game state for the agent
function getState()
  return {
    board = board,
    cursor = { x = cursorX, y = cursorY },
    currentPlayer = currentPlayer,
    gameOver = gameOver,
    score = score,
  }
end
```

Then read it with: `playdate_sim_eval` expression `p __pd_inspect(getState())`

Note: Lua `local` variables are not directly accessible via `playdate_sim_eval`. Only globals and values reachable from globals can be read. When writing game code, expose any state the agent needs to inspect as a global or via `getState()`.

## Environment Setup

edits.newText:
- `patterns.md` -- Common game patterns and idioms

## DAP (Debug Adapter Protocol)

The Playdate Simulator exposes a DAP server on TCP port 55934 for Lua games. The extension connects automatically after `playdate_run_sim`. DAP enables:

- Evaluating Lua expressions (`playdate_sim_eval`)
- Clean screenshots via `playdate.simulator.writeToFile()` (`playdate_screenshot`)
- Direct button callbacks instead of OS keyboard simulation (`playdate_sim_input`)
- Injected `__pd_inspect()` helper for table serialization

DAP is only available for Lua games. C games fall back to OS-level automation (screencapture, osascript keystrokes).

summary:
## Goal
Build a Pi coding agent extension called `pi-playdate` that lets an agent develop Playdate games using the Playdate SDK. Provides typed `playdate_*` tools for building, running, debugging, screenshotting, simulator interaction, and device deployment for Lua and C Playdate projects.  
New expanded goal: investigate and integrate the Playdate Simulator’s built-in Debug Adapter Protocol (DAP) for better simulator control, screenshots, and state inspection.

## Constraints & Preferences
- No bash pass-through for Playdate workflows; every Playdate action should go through typed tools
- UI (`ctx.ui.*`) is for humans; tool results (`details`) are for the LLM
- Device deployment requires `ctx.ui.confirm` every time
- Simulator is the default runtime target
- Cross-platform intent, but macOS is the primary implementation target right now
- Use `@aliou/pi-utils-settings` for config
- Use `@aliou/pi-utils-ui` (latest `^0.2.0`) for tool rendering
- Use `@sinclair/typebox` directly in `dependencies`
- `promptGuidelines` must mention the tool name
- **No `playdate_new_project` tool** — scaffolding is skill-driven from reference templates + `write`
- Template/reference content must be verified against the actual local Playdate SDK docs
- The extension may use `node:child_process` only for the simulator process as a documented exception
- User wants a proper DAP client in the extension before switching simulator operations to DAP
- Need to determine whether DAP should be persistent vs per-call and whether a library is needed

## Progress
### Done
- [x] Package.json with correct deps, bundledDependencies, peerDeps (`"*"` range), pi manifest
- [x] `tsconfig.json`, `biome.json`, repo scaffolding, GitHub Actions, Changesets, Husky, schema generation
- [x] `src/config.ts` — `PlaydateConfig` / `ResolvedPlaydateConfig` with `ConfigLoader`
- [x] `src/lib/state.ts` — ephemeral `RuntimeState` (sim PID, log ring buffer, last build, last device port)
- [x] `src/lib/exec.ts` — thin wrapper around `pi.exec`
- [x] `src/lib/sdk.ts` — SDK path resolution, version reading, pdc/simulator/ARM toolchain discovery
- [x] `src/lib/project.ts` — project kind detection (lua/c/hybrid), pdxinfo, source/output dirs
- [x] `src/lib/pdc.ts` — run pdc, parse diagnostics, added `exitCode`, synthetic fallback error when `pdc` exits non-zero but no structured errors are parsed, broadened parsing for `error: message` / `warning: message`
- [x] `src/lib/cmake.ts` — CMake configure+build, parse gcc diagnostics
- [x] `src/lib/sim.ts` — simulator lifecycle management; fixed macOS launch to run `Playdate Simulator.app/Contents/MacOS/Playdate Simulator` directly instead of `open -a`; added executable resolution helper; kill-by-PID; guarded stale exit handlers
- [x] `src/lib/device.ts` — serial port discovery, data-disk mode, volume mount, pdutil
- [x] `src/tools/doctor.ts`, `build.ts`, `run_sim.ts`, `stop_sim.ts`, `sim_log.ts`, `screenshot.ts`, `run_device.ts`

### In Progress

- [ ] Decide how DAP session state should be tracked in `RuntimeState`
- [ ] Decide whether `playdate_screenshot`, `playdate_sim_input`, and possibly `playdate_sim_log` should switch to DAP-backed implementations for Lua games
- [ ] Determine how much game-state inspection can be generalized through DAP `eval`/`print`
- [ ] Probe local-variable / closure / debug-library access patterns to read game state without screenshots for arbitrary Lua games
- [ ] Evaluate whether DAP works only for Lua projects and how tools should gracefully fall back for C/hybrid projects

### Blocked
- DAP probing on a bad simulator state was misleading because two simulator instances were running simultaneously; after closing both and restarting a single simulator, DAP worked correctly
- Public web research via `scout` was partially blocked by GitHub auth failures (`SCOUT_GITHUB_TOKEN` invalid), but local SDK docs and direct probing were sufficient
- Reading arbitrary game state is not automatic when games store data in `local` variables rather than globals; requires targeted `eval`, debug hooks, or game instrumentation

## Key Decisions
- **No `playdate_new_project` tool**: User prefers skill-driven scaffolding via reference template files + `write`
- **`@sinclair/typebox` in dependencies**: Required for compatibility with `pi-coding-agent`
- **`child_process.spawn` for simulator**: Documented exception for long-lived streaming processes that `pi.exec()` doesn't support
- **Explicit `interface` params over `Static<>` in some tools**: Avoids inference issues with `StringEnum`
- **Use actual SDK docs/templates**: Reference files must match the installed Playdate SDK, not guessed snippets
- **macOS simulator must be launched by real binary, not `open -a`**: `open` tracks the wrong PID and breaks simulator state/logging
- **`pdc` failures need synthetic diagnostics**: Non-zero exit with no parsed errors should still surface a meaningful error
- **Temporary screenshot/input implementation can use macOS automation**: `screencapture`, Swift/CoreGraphics, and `osascript` work as a bridge
- **Preferred long-term simulator integration is DAP for Lua games**: It gives clean screenshots, direct Lua eval, and direct callback invocation without window focus or UI automation
- **No external DAP library is required**: The simulator DAP protocol is simple enough to implement directly with Node `net.Socket`
- **DAP should likely be persistent**: connect once, `initialize` + `configurationDone`, then reuse the socket for many `evaluate` calls instead of opening a fresh TCP connection per tool call
- **DAP is not just “writing commands in a prompt”**: it is proper Debug Adapter Protocol over TCP with framed JSON messages; the REPL behavior is exposed through the DAP `evaluate` request
- **DAP-backed state inspection is feasible for Lua games**: models without vision could potentially inspect game state through `eval` / `print`, but local-variable-heavy games may need debug/upvalue access or explicit serialization helpers

## Next Steps
1. Implement `src/lib/dap.ts` with TCP framing, sequence numbers, `initialize`, `configurationDone`, reconnect logic, and `evaluate()`
2. Extend `RuntimeState` to track DAP connection/session state
3. Add a `playdate_dap_doctor`-style internal capability check or incorporate DAP checks into `playdate_doctor`
4. Migrate `playdate_screenshot` for Lua games to DAP using `playdate.graphics.getDisplayImage()` + `playdate.simulator.writeToFile()`, keep OS fallback for non-DAP cases
5. Migrate `playdate_sim_input` for Lua games to DAP by invoking button callbacks directly; keep osascript fallback where needed
6. Investigate whether simulator log output should come from DAP events/stdout instead of process pipes
7. Probe generalized state extraction patterns for Lua games:
   - globals
   - callback closures / upvalues
   - `debug` library access
   - optional helper serialization
8. Decide how tools should detect and branch between Lua, C, and hybrid projects for DAP features
9. Update docs (`README.md`, `SKILL.md`, `AGENTS.md`) once DAP-backed behavior is implemented
10. Commit and push DAP integration once stable

What changed:

- **DAP now lazy/on-demand**
  - tools no longer expect pre-connected client state
  - `playdate_screenshot`
  - `playdate_sim_input`
  - `playdate_sim_eval`

- **signal now actually used**
  - threaded through:
    - `DapClient.connect(..., signal)`
    - `evaluate(..., signal)`
    - `evalLua(..., signal)`
    - `printExpr(..., signal)`
    - `screenshot(..., signal)`
  - request abort now rejects pending DAP requests
  - connect abort disconnects socket
  - screenshot wait delay is abortable
  - sim input hold delay is abortable

- `src/lib/sim.ts`
- `src/tools/screenshot.ts`
- `src/tools/sim_input.ts`
- `src/tools/sim_eval.ts`

name: playdate
description: Develop games for the Panic Playdate handheld using the pi-playdate extension. Use when the user wants to create, build, run, or debug a Playdate game in Lua or C, work with .pdx bundles, run the Simulator, take screenshots of a running game, or deploy to a connected Playdate device over USB.
---

# Playdate Development

This skill teaches you how to develop games for the Panic Playdate using the `pi-playdate` extension. All Playdate operations go through the `playdate_*` tools -- never shell out to `pdc`, `pdutil`, `cmake`, or any SDK binary directly.

## Available Tools

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `playdate_doctor` | Check SDK installation and environment health |
| `playdate_build` | Compile project to .pdx bundle |
| `playdate_run_sim` | Launch the Playdate Simulator |
| `playdate_stop_sim` | Stop the running simulator |
| `playdate_sim_log` | Read simulator log output |
| `playdate_screenshot` | Capture simulator screenshot |
| `playdate_sim_input` | Send D-pad/A/B/menu input to the simulator |
| `playdate_sim_eval` | Evaluate Lua in the running simulator (read state, run code) |
| `playdate_run_device` | Deploy to a connected Playdate device |

## Creating a New Project

There is no scaffolding tool. Create project files directly using `write`.

Read the appropriate template reference before creating:

- **Lua project**: Read [references/templates-lua.md](references/templates-lua.md) for the required files and their contents.
- **C project**: Read [references/templates-c.md](references/templates-c.md) for the required files, CMakeLists.txt setup, and C API boilerplate.

Every project needs a `Source/pdxinfo` file. See [references/project-layout.md](references/project-layout.md) for the format.

## Typical Workflows

### New game (Lua)

1. Read `references/templates-lua.md`
2. Create `Source/main.lua` and `Source/pdxinfo` using `write`
3. `playdate_build`
4. `playdate_run_sim`
5. `playdate_screenshot` to check visuals
6. `playdate_sim_input` to interact with the game (D-pad, A, B buttons)
7. Edit code, rebuild, repeat

### New game (C)

1. Read `references/templates-c.md`
2. Create `src/main.c`, `Source/pdxinfo`, and `CMakeLists.txt` using `write`
3. `playdate_build` (auto-detects C project and uses CMake)
4. `playdate_run_sim`

### Debug loop

1. `playdate_build` -- check `details.errors` for issues
2. If errors, fix the source files and rebuild
3. `playdate_run_sim` to test
4. `playdate_sim_log` to check runtime output
5. `playdate_screenshot` to verify visuals
6. `playdate_sim_eval` to inspect game state at runtime
7. Iterate

### Deploy to device

1. `playdate_build` with target "device"
2. `playdate_run_device` (always prompts user for confirmation)

### Interacting with a running game

1. `playdate_sim_input` to send D-pad, A, B, or menu button presses
2. `playdate_screenshot` to see the current display (clean 400x240, no chrome)
3. `playdate_sim_eval` to read or modify game state at runtime

`playdate_sim_input`, `playdate_screenshot`, and `playdate_sim_eval` all require DAP (Debug Adapter Protocol). DAP connects automatically when the simulator starts a Lua game. These tools only work with Lua games -- C games do not support DAP.

### Reading game state without vision

For models without vision or when you need structured data:

- Use `playdate_sim_eval` with `p <expression>` to read values: `p score`, `p playerX`
- Use `__pd_inspect(table)` to pretty-print tables: `p __pd_inspect(board)`
- `__pd_inspect` is injected automatically by the extension -- no game code changes needed

For richer state access, add a `getState()` global to the game during scaffolding:

```lua
-- Expose game state for the agent
function getState()
  return {
    board = board,
    cursor = { x = cursorX, y = cursorY },
    currentPlayer = currentPlayer,
    gameOver = gameOver,
    score = score,
  }
end
```

Then read it with: `playdate_sim_eval` expression `p __pd_inspect(getState())`

Note: Lua `local` variables are not directly accessible via `playdate_sim_eval`. Only globals and values reachable from globals can be read. When writing game code, expose any state the agent needs to inspect as a global or via `getState()`.

## Environment Setup

Run `playdate_doctor` first to verify the SDK is installed and configured. If the SDK path is not auto-detected, the user can set it via `/playdate:settings`.

## Reference Files

For API details, read the reference files in this skill's `references/` directory:

- `project-layout.md` -- Playdate project structure and pdxinfo format
- `templates-lua.md` -- Lua project template with minimal playdate.update()
- `templates-c.md` -- C project template with CMakeLists.txt and event handler
- `lua-api.md` -- Lua API quick reference
- `c-api.md` -- C API quick reference
- `corelibs.md` -- Standard Lua libraries (sprites, graphics, timers, etc.)
- `performance.md` -- Performance tips for the Playdate hardware
- `patterns.md` -- Common game patterns and idioms

## DAP (Debug Adapter Protocol)

The Playdate Simulator exposes a DAP server on TCP port 55934 for Lua games. The extension connects automatically after `playdate_run_sim`. DAP enables:

- Evaluating Lua expressions (`playdate_sim_eval`)
- Clean screenshots via `playdate.simulator.writeToFile()` (`playdate_screenshot`)
- Direct button callbacks instead of OS keyboard simulation (`playdate_sim_input`)
- Injected `__pd_inspect()` helper for table serialization

DAP is only available for Lua games. C games can still be built and run, but interactive tools (screenshot, input, eval) require DAP and will not work.

- `release` -- release a held button

`playdate_sim_input`, `playdate_screenshot`, and `playdate_sim_eval` all require DAP (Debug Adapter Protocol). DAP connects automatically when the simulator starts a Lua game. These tools only work with Lua games -- C games do not support DAP.

### Playing a game autonomously

For visual play:

1. Use `playdate_screenshot` to read the current screen
2. Decide the next move
3. Use `playdate_sim_input` to send that move
4. Use `playdate_screenshot` again to verify the result
5. Repeat until the game ends

For state-driven play without vision:

1. Use `playdate_sim_eval` to inspect the current state
2. Decide the next move from the returned values
3. Use `playdate_sim_input` to send that move
4. Use `playdate_sim_eval` again to confirm the new state
5. Repeat until the game ends

Common `playdate_sim_input` examples:
- move cursor right: `button: "right"`
- move cursor down twice: `button: "down", repeat: 2`
- confirm/select: `button: "a"`
- cancel/back: `button: "b"`
- open menu: `button: "menu"`

are there tools to restart the simulator / rebuild ?

Yes.

Existing tools:
- `playdate_build` — rebuild project
- `playdate_run_sim` — launch simulator with a `.pdx`
- `playdate_stop_sim` — stop simulator

Also:
- calling **`playdate_run_sim` again effectively restarts the simulator**
  - it goes through `spawnSimulator()`
  - that kills any existing tracked simulator first

So today the restart/rebuild flow is:

- rebuild: `playdate_build`
- restart sim: `playdate_run_sim`
- full explicit restart: `playdate_stop_sim` -> `playdate_run_sim`

What does **not** exist yet:
- no dedicated `playdate_restart_sim` tool
- no single combined `build + restart` tool

content.text:
Short answer: **probably not a reliable built-in simulator log file** to depend on.

Current state in `pi-playdate`:
- `src/lib/sim.ts` already captures simulator `stdout`/`stderr`
- it stores lines in `state.simLogBuffer`
- `playdate_sim_log` just reads that in-memory ring buffer

So today logging is:
- **stream-backed**
- **session-local**
- **not file-backed**
- **not watcher/alert-backed**

If you want behavior like `pi-processes` log watches, best options are:

## Best option: watch the stream directly
Don’t poll a file.

Since we already own the spawned simulator process, we can:
- match log lines as they arrive from `child.stdout` / `child.stderr`
- trigger notifications / agent turns on patterns
- keep same ring buffer for manual reads

That’s closer to `pi-processes` than polling a file, and better:
- no fs polling lag
- no rotation issues
- no stale file path issues
- works even if simulator never writes a log file

## Second-best option: tee logs to our own file
If you want persistence/debuggability, we can also:
- create a temp/session log file
- append every captured stdout/stderr line to it
- expose the path in tool details
- optionally tail/poll that file ourselves

This would be **our file**, not a simulator-native one.

That gives:
- stable artifact for inspection
- easier postmortem/debugging
- possible future `playdate_sim_watch` / alerting logic

## What I would not do
I would not build around “maybe the simulator writes logs somewhere on disk” unless we verify:
- exact path
- platform behavior
- whether Lua `print()` always lands there
- whether it’s per-session or global
- whether it exists on macOS/Linux consistently

Given what the code does now, **the extension-controlled stream is the reliable source of truth**.

## Recommendation
Implement watcher behavior on top of the existing stream capture:

- add config/runtime watch rules, eg:
  - `error`
  - `assert`
  - custom regex
- on each new log line in `pushLogLine()` or `onData`
  - test patterns
  - debounce/repeat rules
  - notify user / maybe surface agent turn

If you also want inspectable artifacts:
- tee the same lines to `~/Library/Caches/...` or `/tmp/pi-playdate-<session>.log`

So:
- **yes**, we can have something watcher-like
- **no**, I would not base it on a simulator-owned log file unless we prove one exists and is stable
- the clean design is: **watch stdout/stderr directly, optionally mirror to our own file**

If you want, I can implement:
1. a session log file in `sim.ts`
2. `playdate_sim_log` returning the file path too
3. simple watch rules for `error|warning|panic|traceback` lines

## 1) How simulator logging is handled

Short answer: **it does not watch a log file**.  
It uses two mechanisms:

### a) Task/command output (stdout-ish, via VS Code terminal UI)
The extension’s task runners write their own status messages into a pseudoterminal (`TaskRunnerTerminal`), which prints lines into the VS Code terminal output when tasks run.

- `TaskRunnerTerminal` emits messages via `onDidWrite` and runs one `TaskRunner` implementation. ([src/core/TaskRunnerTerminal.ts](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/src/core/TaskRunnerTerminal.ts))
- `PDCTaskRunner`, `SimulatorMacOSTaskRunner`, `SimulatorWin32TaskRunner`, `SimulatorLinuxTaskRunner` all call `onMessage(...)` and command execution/spawn APIs, then rely on that terminal emitter for visible logs. ([src/pdc/PDCTaskRunner.ts](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/src/pdc/PDCTaskRunner.ts), [src/simulator/SimulatorMacOSTaskRunner.ts](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/src/simulator/SimulatorMacOSTaskRunner.ts), [src/simulator/SimulatorWin32TaskRunner.ts](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/src/simulator/SimulatorWin32TaskRunner.ts), [src/simulator/SimulatorLinuxTaskRunner.ts](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/src/simulator/SimulatorLinuxTaskRunner.ts))

### b) Optional debug-protocol traffic logging
When `logDebugAdapter: true` in launch config, the proxy logs raw DAP messages from both sides to a dedicated output channel (“Playdate Debug”).

- Debug logger: `DebugAdapterLogger` appends tagged client/server messages with timestamps into `vscode` output channel. ([src/debug/DebugAdapterLogger.ts](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/src/debug/DebugAdapterLogger.ts))
- Proxy uses it in `ProxyServer` for both client→server and server→client byte streams (before transform). ([src/debug/ProxyServer.ts](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/src/debug/ProxyServer.ts))

### c) Notable: no file tailing for simulator logs
There is no file watcher (`fs.watch` / file-tail) for simulator logs in the code. The simulator is started as a process with `exec/spawn` and detached/no-stdio streaming semantics; logs aren’t consumed from its stdout stream by the extension. ([src/simulator/SimulatorWin32TaskRunner.ts](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/src/simulator/SimulatorWin32TaskRunner.ts), [src/simulator/SimulatorLinuxTaskRunner.ts](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/src/simulator/SimulatorLinuxTaskRunner.ts), [src/simulator/SimulatorMacOSTaskRunner.ts](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/src/simulator/SimulatorMacOSTaskRunner.ts))

So: **it’s command/task output + optional DAP message capture, not file watching.**

---

## 2) Overall features (everything exposed by extension)

### Core advertised features
From README:
- Debug Lua code in Playdate Simulator
- Build `.pdx` using `pdc`
- Problem matchers for `pdc`
- Open Playdate Simulator
- Run/debug current Lua file from editor toolbar ([README.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/README.md))

### Command palette / editor toolbar
- `playdate-debug.runEditorContents`  
- `playdate-debug.debugEditorContents`
- Registered in menu + toolbar for Lua files ([package.json](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/package.json))

### Tasks and task providers
- Custom task type `pdc` (Build)
- Custom task type `playdate-simulator` (Run)
- Problem matchers:
  - `$pdc-lua`
  - `$pdc-external` ([package.json](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/package.json))

### Debug provider/launcher
- Debugger type `playdate`
- Supports `launch` (and `attach` config options are declared)
- Workspace settings for:
  - `playdate-debug.sdkPath`
  - `playdate-debug.sourcePath`
  - `playdate-debug.outputPath`
  - `playdate-debug.productName`
- `debug` configuration attributes:
  - `logDebugAdapter`
  - `disableWorkarounds`
  - `retryTimeout`
  - `maxRetries`
- Debug configuration provider that resolves runtime values (SDK path/version/source/game path) from env/settings/workspace ([package.json](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/package.json), [src/core/ConfigurationResolver.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/core/ConfigurationResolver.ts), [src/debug/PlaydateDebugConfigurationProvider.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/debug/PlaydateDebugConfigurationProvider.ts))

### PDC task options
- `strip`, `noCompress`, `verbose`, `quiet`, `skipUnknown`
- `incrementBuildNumber`
- `libPath`
- custom `sourcePath`, `gamePath`, `sdkPath`
- uses `-sdkpath` always and command generation in task runner ([package.json](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/package.json), [src/pdc/PDCExecutionFactory.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/pdc/PDCExecutionFactory.ts), [src/pdc/getPDCCommand.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/pdc/getPDCCommand.ts), [src/core/incrementBuildNumber.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/core/incrementBuildNumber.ts))

### Simulator task options
- `openGame` (default true)
- `kill` (kill existing simulator first)
- `argv` passthrough to game launch
- Platform-specific launching and kill commands ([package.json](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/package.json), [src/simulator/SimulatorExecutionFactory.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/simulator/SimulatorExecutionFactory.ts), [src/simulator/SimulatorMacOSTaskRunner.ts](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/src/simulator/SimulatorMacOSTaskRunner.ts), [src/simulator/SimulatorWin32TaskRunner.ts](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/src/simulator/SimulatorWin32TaskRunner.ts), [src/simulator/SimulatorLinuxTaskRunner.ts](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/src/simulator/SimulatorLinuxTaskRunner.ts))

### Convenience and automation
- Auto-resolve SDK/source/output/game paths (or workspace settings override)
- Can build-run-debug current Lua file quickly (main.lua workflow)
- Stops prior debug sessions before starting a new one (`DebugSessionRegistry`)
- Multi-root workspace-friendly path resolution logic ([src/core/ConfigurationResolver.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/core/ConfigurationResolver.ts), [src/editor/EditorContentsCommand.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/editor/EditorContentsCommand.ts), [src/editor/DebugSessionRegistry.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/editor/DebugSessionRegistry.ts), [src/core/getWorkspaceRoot.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/core/getWorkspaceRoot.ts))

---

## 3) How it interacts with the simulator (DAP, commands, etc.)

### Build + launch flow
- `pdc` task builds `.pdx` via SDK `pdc` binary.
- `playdate-simulator` task starts simulator with resolved game path / args.
- Debug launch uses a **custom debug adapter descriptor factory** that starts a **local proxy server** and returns a `DebugAdapterServer` port to VS Code. ([src/pdc/PDCTaskRunner.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/pdc/PDCTaskRunner.ts), [src/simulator/SimulatorTaskProvider.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/simulator/SimulatorTaskProvider.ts), [src/debug/ProxyDebugAdapterDescriptorFactory.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/debug/ProxyDebugAdapterDescriptorFactory.ts))

### Debug transport / protocol path
- Simulator debug interface listens on TCP **55934** (`SIMULATOR_DEBUG_PORT`). ([src/constants.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/constants.ts))
- Proxy connects to that port via retry logic (`waitForDebugPort`) then starts local socket server; VS Code connects to local proxy port.
- DAP messages are manually framed/parsed with `Content-Length` header + `\r\n\r\n` separator and proxied both ways. ([src/util/waitForDebugPort.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/util/waitForDebugPort.ts), [src/debug/ProxyServer.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/debug/ProxyServer.ts))

### Platform-specific simulator launch commands
- macOS: `open` Playdate Simulator app (`/usr/bin/open -a`) with optional game path + `--args`.
- Windows: `PlaydateSimulator.exe`, optionally `tasklist` check + `taskkill`.
- Linux: `PlaydateSimulator` binary, optional `pidof` check + kill command.
- Kill command helper varies by platform. ([src/simulator/getMacOSSimulatorCommand.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/simulator/getMacOSSimulatorCommand.ts), [src/simulator/SimulatorMacOSTaskRunner.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/simulator/SimulatorMacOSTaskRunner.ts), [src/simulator/SimulatorWin32TaskRunner.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/simulator/SimulatorWin32TaskRunner.ts), [src/simulator/SimulatorLinuxTaskRunner.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/simulator/SimulatorLinuxTaskRunner.ts), [src/simulator/getKillSimulatorCommand.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/simulator/getKillSimulatorCommand.ts))

---

## 4) Interesting implementation details (debugging, logs, sim communication)

### DAP proxy + protocol compatibility fixes
The extension doesn’t directly plug VS Code into simulator; it inserts a proxy layer to patch protocol quirks:

- `FixLaunchResponse` and `FixRestartResponse` synthesize responses (and sequence offsets) because simulator behavior differs from what VS Code expects.
- `FixSupportsRestartRequest` / `FixSupportsTerminateRequest` mutate `initialize` response capabilities to avoid unsupported methods.
- `FixVariablesReference` injects `variablesReference: 0` when absent.
- `FixBreakpointVerified` marks breakpoints as verified in responses.
- All fixes are optional via `disableWorkarounds`. They auto-disable for SDK >= `1.13.0`. ([src/debug/fix/Fixer.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/debug/fix/Fixer.ts), [src/debug/fix/FixLaunchResponse.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/debug/fix/FixLaunchResponse.ts), [src/debug/fix/FixRestartResponse.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/debug/fix/FixRestartResponse.ts), [src/debug/fix/FixSupportsRestartRequest.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/debug/fix/FixSupportsRestartRequest.ts), [src/debug/fix/FixSupportsTerminateRequest.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/debug/fix/FixSupportsTerminateRequest.ts), [src/debug/fix/FixVariablesReference.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/debug/fix/FixVariablesReference.ts), [src/debug/fix/FixBreakpointVerified.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/debug/fix/FixBreakpointVerified.ts), [src/debug/fix/FixerFactory.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/debug/fix/FixerFactory.ts), [src/debug/ProxyDebugAdapterDescriptorFactory.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/debug/ProxyDebugAdapterDescriptorFactory.ts), [src/constants.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/constants.ts))

### Debugger reliability behavior
- `waitForDebugPort` retry loop before connecting avoids race with simulator startup.
- Retry options are configurable through launch config (`retryTimeout`, `maxRetries`), defaulting to small timeout/retry count. ([src/util/waitForDebugPort.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/util/waitForDebugPort.ts))

### Version/platform guards
- Non-mac debug launch is blocked for older SDK versions (before `1.13.0`) unless supported.
- For run/debug-current-file flow, if unsupported it still runs build+sim launch but skips debug attach. ([src/core/ConfigurationResolver.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/core/ConfigurationResolver.ts), [src/debug/PlaydateDebugConfigurationProvider.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/debug/PlaydateDebugConfigurationProvider.ts), [src/editor/EditorContentsCommand.ts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/main/src/editor/EditorContentsCommand.ts))

---

---
title: Useful Links for Playdate Development - Playdate Help
description: A list of links to video tutorials, code libraries, and other helpful resources for Playdate developers.
image: https://help.play.date/images/card-Playdate-help-library-2.png
---

# [ Useful Links for Playdate Development](/developer/dev-links/) 

Amazing people around the world are putting together video tutorials, code libraries, and other helpful resources for Playdate developers. Here’s our roundup of some we’ve seen. Please note that this information doesn’t come from Panic, and it’s not an officially supported part of the Playdate SDK.

## Learning to program Playdate

* **[The Complete Beginners Guide to Playdate Game Development](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UZ04rk3lLqU) by SquidGod.** Complete tutorial on making games for Playdate using Lua and the Playdate SDK. Covers environment setup, code, and helpful resources.
* **[Getting Started with the Playdate SDK: Setup and Basics](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J0ufxinp7No) by SquidGod.** 12-minute video on setting up the Playdate SDK for Windows and putting together a simple game.
* **[Everything About Playdate SDK Collisions in 7 Minutes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=27vCPiwgWzQ) by SquidGod.** 7-minute video on collisions.
* **[Object Oriented Programming for the Playdate SDK](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e9x6DsWk-IU) by SquidGod.** 13-minute video on object oriented programming for Playdate.
* **[Making a Roguelike for the Playdate](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v9YBJCAa3EQ) by SquidGod.** 3-minute video starting a development log for this game project.
* **[The Beginner’s Guide to Lua for Game Development](https://squidgod.itch.io/lua-for-game-development) by SquidGod.** A book that will take you from a complete beginner to knowing the basics of coding in Lua.
* **[SquidGod’s YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/@SquidGodDev)** has more Playdate tutorials!
* **[Compiling Lua projects on Windows ](https://devforum.play.date/t/tutorial-compiling-lua-projects-on-windows/3332) by Tim Hei.**
* **[Playdate game development in C](https://rua.ua.es/dspace/bitstream/10045/117000/1/Playdate%5Fgame%5Fdevelopment%5Fin%5FC%5FBenavent%5FRamon%5FAlberto.pdf) by Alberto Benavent Ramón.** 87-page PDF of a Bachelor’s Thesis in Multimedia Engineering.

## Books

* **[Programming the Panic Playdate in Lua](https://www.amazon.com/Programming-Panic-Playdate-Ronald-Tanikawa/dp/B0DV96VQYQ) by Ronald Tanikawa.** Covers everything a budding Playdate Lua developer needs to know: crank APIs, sprites, music, fonts, tilemaps, and much more.
* **[Make Games for Playdate with Lua](https://leanpub.com/playdatebook) by Brett Chalupa.** Includes example games downloadable from [Github](https://github.com/brettchalupa/playdatebook).
* **[Game Design Document: A Game Development Document for the Design of 1BIT Video Games and Experiences](https://www.amazon.com/Game-Design-Document-Development-Experiences/dp/B0FP9P3MXH/ref=sr%5F1%5F1?crid=ZLGHJSRO8YY4&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.OUxxAvGvLMPHqbsoQ2wKeQ.jTLjKh5L5ieBTRjiOUbfQqVYIwJEYba-Js1uXe8NTPU&dib%5Ftag=se&keywords=playdate+console+book&qid=1757365953&sprefix=playdate+console+boo%2Caps%2C129&sr=8-1) by Brian Jameson.** A beautiful, blank notebook for all of your Playdate game ideas. Includes templates for sprites, tiles, game mechanics… you name it.

## Libraries

* **[Timeline for Playdate](https://github.com/mierau/playdate-timeline) by Dustin Mierau.**A Lua library designed to make it easier to compose animations and events in your game code over time. See some of Dustin’s remarkable animations at work in [_Playmaker_](https://play.date/games/playmaker/).
* **[Noble Engine](https://github.com/NobleRobot/NobleEngine) by Mark LaCroix.**A li’l game engine for Playdate.
* **[AnimatedSprite](https://github.com/Whitebrim/AnimatedSprite) by Whitebrim.** Sprite class extension that covers animations, finite state machine, and JSON loading.
* **[Taxman Engine](https://github.com/McDevon/taxman-engine) by Jussi Enroos.** 2D Game Engine for Playdate and other platforms.
* **[Panels](https://github.com/cadin/panels) by Cadin Batrack.** Build interactive comics for the Playdate console.
* **[A list of helpful libraries and code](https://devforum.play.date/t/a-list-of-helpful-libraries-and-code/221) by Dev Forum members.** A thread of helpful libraries and small bits of code, started and maintained by our Dev Forum members.

## Coding Tools

* **[Nova](https://nova.app) by Panic.** You can use any code editor you like with our SDK. We happen to make a pretty nice one for macOS, and it’s great for Playdate development, with easy building and debugging.
* **[pdmanager](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/pdmanager/id6751735648) by Keith Baker.** Mac app that connects to and lets you manage your Playdate—organize games, back up saves, track achivements, and more.
* **[Playdate Debug for VS Code](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug) by midouest.** Unofficial Playdate debug extension for Visual Studio Code on macOS, Windows and Ubuntu.
* **[VS Code Playdate Template (Windows & Linux)](https://github.com/Whitebrim/VSCode-PlaydateTemplate) by Whitebrim.** A template for autocompletion and running your code in the Playdate Simulator on Windows and Linux.
* **[Playdate VS Code Template (Mac)](https://github.com/cadin/playdate-vscode-template) by Cadin Batrack.** VS Code template with tasks for building and running in Playdate simulator on macOS.
* **[Playdate Types](https://github.com/balpha/playdate-types) by Benjamin Dumke-von der Ehe.** Type annotations for the Playdate Lua SDK.
* **[LuaCATS](https://github.com/notpeter/playdate-luacats) by Peter Tripp.** LuaCATS is a way to provide machine-readable Lua type annotations and comments, enabling inline autocompletion and linting suggestions.

## Graphics & Fonts

* **[Caps](https://play.date/caps) by Panic.** Panic’s official bitmap-font editor for Playdate fonts. Draw your own typographic characters, edit existing fonts, kern and preview them—all right here.
* **[Playdate Arcade Fonts](https://github.com/idleberg/playdate-arcade-fonts) by Jan T. Sott.** A growing collection of bitmap fonts based on classic arcade games.
* **[Playdate Art: Scale](https://donaldhays.com/2019/12/30/playdate-art-scale/) by Donald Hays.** Thoughts and observations on Playdate art, with a focus on choosing the size to make your art tiles and sprites.
* **[Tophat](https://kaasiand.cool/tophat/) by Kaasiand.** A powerful tool to create bitmap fonts for use with the Playdate SDK.
* **[PDFontTool](https://github.com/abenokobo/PDFontTool) by Takuya.** Command line tool for Windows that converts Windows-supported fonts such as TrueType Font, OpenType Font, etc. into fonts for Playdate.

## Languages

* **[Byte-sized Swift: Building Tiny Games for the Playdate](https://www.swift.org/blog/byte-sized-swift-tiny-games-playdate/) by the Swift Team.** The Swift team’s new embedded language support means you can target platforms like Playdate via Swift.
* **[PlaydateKit](https://github.com/finnvoor/PlaydateKit) by Finn Voorhees.** Swift bindings for the Playdate C SDK.
* **[Crankscript](https://github.com/crankscript/crankscript)**. A rich framework allowing devs to author Playdate games in TypeScript.
* **[Playdate-C++](https://github.com/nstbayless/playdate-cpp) by Metaphaseaudio.** C++ on Playdate.
* **[Playdate C++ Extensions](https://github.com/metaphaseaudio/playdate-cpp-extensions) by Metaphaseaudio.** Classes and functions to assist with development for the Playdate in C++.
* **[Rust for Playdate](https://github.com/pd-rs/crankstart) by Rob Tsuk and Alexander Koz.** “A barely functional, wildly incomplete and basically undocumented Rust crate whose aim is to let you write Games for the Playdate handheld gaming system in Rust.”
* **[Go for Playdate](https://github.com/playdate-go/pdgo) by Roman Bielyi.** _pdgo_ is an open-source project providing Go compiler support, SDK bindings, tools, and examples for developing games and applications on Playdate.
* **[Nim Playdate](https://github.com/samdze/playdate-nim) by Samuele Zolfanelli.** Nim bindings with extra features for the Playdate SDK.
* **[Zig Template for Playdate](https://github.com/DanB91/Zig-Playdate-Template) by DanB91.** Use this template as a starting point to write your Playdate games in Zig.

## Devlogs

* **[_Atlantic ‘41_](https://stephanrewind.itch.io/atlantic-41) by Stephan Rewind.** A tremendously detailed World War 2 U-boat simulation.
* **[_Diora_](https://dioragame.com/devlog/) by Zachary Snyder.** Devlog of an isometric 3D game.
* **[_Mars After Midnight_ development log](https://dukope.itch.io/mars-after-midnight) by Lucas Pope.** _Papers, Please_ and _Return of the Obra Dinn_’s creator’s posts about the development of his Playdate game.
* **[_Pullfrog_ development log](https://amano.games/devlog) by Amano Games.** Tetris meets frog.

## Playdate Resources Elsewhere

* **[Playdate Stuff](https://github.com/stars/filmgirl/lists/playdate-stuff) by Christina Warren.** Cool Things for Panic’s Playdate.
* **[Awesome Playdate](https://github.com/sayhiben/awesome-playdate) by Ben Menesini.** A list of awesome resources for Playdate game development and the Playdate SDK.
* **[SDK Resources](https://playdate-wiki.com/wiki/Developing%5Ffor%5FPlaydate) by Playdate Community Wiki.** A list of resources that are available for free to help you with developing games on Playdate.

## Pulp

We also have a list of resources you may find helpful when making games in [Pulp](/developer/pulp-links).

[If you didn't find an answer above, contact us](/contact/)

# Playdate Debug

[![tests](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/actions/workflows/tests.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/actions/workflows/tests.yaml)

Unofficial Playdate debug extension for Visual Studio Code on macOS, Windows and Ubuntu

## Features

* Debug Lua code running in the Playdate Simulator
* Compile games to `.pdx` using `pdc`
* Problem matchers for `pdc`
* Open the Playdate Simulator
* Run and debug current Lua file in the Playdate Simulator from the editor toolbar

## Requirements

* The [Playdate SDK](https://play.date/dev/) must be installed separately

## Quick setup

### Tasks and debug launcher

Copy the following `.vscode/tasks.json` and `.vscode/launch.json` configuration:

// .vscode/tasks.json
{
  "version": "2.0.0",
  "tasks": [
    {
      "type": "pdc",
      "problemMatcher": ["$pdc-lua", "$pdc-external"],
      "label": "Playdate: Build"
    },
    {
      "type": "playdate-simulator",
      "problemMatcher": ["$pdc-external"],
      "label": "Playdate: Run"
    },
    {
      "label": "Playdate: Build and Run",
      "dependsOn": ["Playdate: Build", "Playdate: Run"],
      "dependsOrder": "sequence",
      "problemMatcher": [],
      "group": {
        "kind": "build",
        "isDefault": true
      }
    }
  ]
}

// .vscode/launch.json
{
  "version": "0.2.0",
  "configurations": [
    {
      "type": "playdate",
      "request": "launch",
      "name": "Playdate: Debug",
      "preLaunchTask": "${defaultBuildTask}"
    }
  ]
}

The debugger can be launched from the "Run and Debug view" by selecting the "Playdate: Debug" launch configuration and then clicking the "Start Debugging" button.

[![Run and Debug view](/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/raw/main/images/run-and-debug-view.png)](/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/images/run-and-debug-view.png)

[![Start Debugging](/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/raw/main/images/start-debugging.png)](/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/images/start-debugging.png)

A [cookiecutter project template](https://github.com/midouest/cookiecutter-playdate) is available for quickly generating new projects with the above configuration from the command line.

See the [basic configuration example](/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/fixtures/workspace/basic-configuration) for more information.

### Run and debug current Lua file

**NOTE:** The "Run/Debug file in Playdate Simulator" command is intended to be a shortcut for prototyping and learning. It is recommended to use the [task and launch configuration above](#tasks-and-debug-launcher).

The extension can build, run and debug the current Lua file in the editor with zero configuration as long the [automatic configuration conditions](#automatic) are met.

When you open a Lua file in the editor after installing the extension, you will now see a launch icon and dropdown menu in the editor toolbar. Clicking the launch icon or selecting an item from the dropdown menu will build and run the current Lua file in the Playdate Simulator. The "Debug file in Playdate Simulator" option will enable breakpoints to be hit.

[![Tooltip](/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/raw/main/images/tooltip.png)](/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/images/tooltip.png)

[![Dropdown Menu](/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/raw/main/images/dropdown-menu.png)](/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/images/dropdown-menu.png)

## Configuration

### Automatic

The tasks and debugger will attempt to automatically resolve the correct configuration using the environment. One of the following conditions must be met for this to work:

* The `PLAYDATE_SDK_PATH` environment variable is set to the Playdate SDK path
* `~/.Playdate/config` exists and the `SDKRoot` property is set to the Playdate SDK path (macOS only)

### Workspace settings override

The default behavior can be overridden by setting the SDK path, game source path, compiled game path or game name in your workspace's `settings.json` file. The extension will fall back to the default behavior for any configuration fields that are not set.

// .vscode/settings.json
{
  "playdate-debug.sdkPath": "/path/to/PlaydateSDK",
  "playdate-debug.sourcePath": "/path/to/MyGame/source",
  "playdate-debug.outputPath": "/path/to/MyGame",
  "playdate-debug.productName": "My Game"
}

See the [override configuration example](/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/fixtures/workspace/override-configuration) for more information about these properties.

### PDC task

See the [pdc configuration example](/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/fixtures/workspace/pdc-configuration) for additional `pdc` task properties.

### Playdate Simulator task

See the [playdate simulator configuration example](/midouest/vscode-playdate-debug/blob/main/fixtures/workspace/playdate-simulator-configuration) for additional `playdate-simulator` task properties.
